utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Summary paragraph 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B-083, in the course of your time at the Ministry of Defence, just in general, did you see there any of the following people: Did you see Goran Hadzic there ever? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man known as Arkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man known as Captain Dragan, Dragan Vasiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on, in which place or office did you see those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them in the building of the Ministry of Defence, which was in Nemanjina Street, number 11, where the government of the Republic of Serbia has its offices today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 55. How many times did you see Arkan; once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Arkan twice. Once I had no contact with him. The second time, I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dragan Vasiljkovic, did you see him once or twice? Once or more than once, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him twice; once in 1991 and once in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Finally, then, of this part of your evidence, paragraph 66, in fact at the top of page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see Exhibit 507, his Exhibits, tab 4. The Chamber sees that this is a document purporting to come from the Republic of Serbian Krajina's Ministry of Defence going to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia in September 1992. The Chamber will see at the end of the document that there's a reference to money from the above work organisations is to be transferred "to our Knin account" or "our transfer account in Knin" from their accounts in Knin, and it says: "We are forced to work in this way because of the cessation of transfer of payments between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." And the body of the document has reference to various businesses and sums of money. The document appears to have been sent to Lieutenant Colonel Jelic, and at this stage all I ask of this witness is this, and it comes from Colonel Spanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just yes or no: Did Lieutenant Colonel Jelic work at the Ministry of Defence at some stage, to your knowledge? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And his responsibility was to carry this through. I assume he did so, but we can't say from this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now seek for this witness, in respect of some other matters, private session. I can point Your Honour to the first paragraph where that would arise, and I can address the justification perhaps itself in private session, with your leave, but it starts at paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I raise it now as it's probably as good a place as any. It concerns the timing and the order of witnesses. The Prosecution are masters of their own agenda for their own purposes. For the accused who receives the weekly witness list, the order of witnesses is no doubt very important in terms of his preparation, and the times that are given as total times on the witness list are also very important because, by that, he is able to put together a system to establish his working pattern, and I should imagine those working with him divide their time appropriately and concentrate on a schedule of time that is indicated by the witness list, and they move no doubt from one topic to another as the weekly witnesses are heard. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And it is very important, I should imagine, for their preparation that the order of witnesses is kept to - and I raise this now because there was talk yesterday of Mrs. Budding being inserted above a Rule 92 bis witness - but also in relation to the time available to him, because he, no doubt, conscious of the Court view of time in this case prepares his cross-examination for what appears the allotted span on the witness list, and so the material that is given to him, no doubt, and the matters that he has to consider are based on that allocated space of time in the weekly schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think it has been made plain before that, as far as the times are concerned, nobody can be bound by what the Prosecution estimate as to the time for each witness. It's merely an estimate. And if he's relying on it, he's been told before and he shouldn't do so. But we will return to the order, which I take the point on, that continual changes of order make preparation difficult. Of course I understand that. As far as timing is concerned, we have to have regard to the overall time that this case is taking. Of course, in a sense, the Prosecution are responsible for the number of witnesses and the length of time that's taken over them. They've called all these witnesses, and it's therefore not surprising that things take a long time. I think this is the 214th, by my calculation, and we have the autumn to go. But still, we have to have in mind time. Is the answer not this: That the accused should be allowed time, but his time must be used reasonably. He can't, for instance, concentrate and argue with the witnesses, as he does, and then complain afterwards that his time is restricted, he's not able to perhaps ask some important questions at the end. If he concentrated on that, he'd get on better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think that that is a matter of technique that experienced advocates would understand how to fit things -- something into a pint pot or litre pot, whatever it should be. The issue here can be, for him, that if the Prosecution, particularly with Mr. Nice, who can go like an express train from the starting station to the end terminus and do witnesses very rapidly in a short period of time, getting over a large amount of information, there is concern here that this can rebound against the accused who would get lesser than otherwise because there are different skills that are at play here and cannot deal with all the topics in the time -- his time is accordingly shortened because of the apparent brevity of the Prosecutor in dealing with these issues very, very rapidly. And I say that so the Trial Chamber can bear that in mind when considering this issue on behalf of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He gets longer with slower counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It is noticeable that it has that effect. And Mr. Nice probably takes the most important witnesses. We go back to the witness Kucan, who was quite an important, significant witness, and he was done in a day. Well, we've had less important people here who have been days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Surely the point is that it is the content of the evidence and the substance of the evidence that is important rather than the length of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with that, and that is why I'm saying length of Prosecutor here, for the accused, may not be an indicator, because Mr. Nice is capable of getting in a vast amount of detail in a short period of time. I don't want to discourage him, and I don't want to use up too much time myself, but I do say this because it's important to bear this in mind with the litigant in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My only observation, Your Honour, would be that I hope I, and indeed my colleagues, are progressively simply narrowing the focus onto the critical pieces of evidence, and we would press the Chamber -- or press the accused and the amici, through the Chamber, to focus their cross-examination accordingly. And I would respectfully submit that the accused has shown himself to have rapidly developed the skills of cross-examination, and as he frequently reveals by the end parts of his cross-examinations, when forced to it, he does understand what has to be dealt with by way of joining issues. It's rather sad sometimes, that he gets there -- sad from our point of view, that he gets there at the end rather than at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: An hour and a quarter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I suppose this is not something for the closed session or a private session, discussing the establishment where this witness worked. I'm not going to ask him any identifying questions. And I believe it was in open session that the matter of where he worked, where he was employed, was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That was mentioned in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 83, I would like to go through very briefly a couple of matters. [redacted], [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is something that will almost -- a matter for the witness, but it may well transgress the protection measures in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That matter was dealt with in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness 83, since we are now again in open session, would you please look at these two statements of yours from -- the 2001 and 2002 one in which there isn't a single paragraph in either of these statements without deletions or corrections or notes made by you that it is incorrect, that it is erroneously interpreted, that there are errors, et cetera, et cetera. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And I did that because that -- I had the occasion to receive those statements in the Serbian language, the things I said. And it is my conviction that I didn't say that in that way and I feel that it is not in order for these charges to be made against you, and I explained to them and the Tribunal that I think it is not fair for us to discuss something that I myself think is not correct. And I think it's a waste of time for the Court, because I say quite plainly that there are errors of such a nature that I couldn't under any circumstances sign such a statement. The people realise this now, and what we were saying today I wrote in my own hand. If I had written such a statement in my own hand, I would stand by it, but believe me, many of these things would not have been said if that had been the procedure, especially as there are some things that are absolutely untrue. For instance, that story about a car that I heard from some secretary somewhere and then I told them about it, but I wouldn't have allowed it to be entered into such a document. If I had known it would have been, I would not have allowed them to do it. I asked them to show these corrections to you in time so that we wouldn't need to discuss them. These are technical errors and things that absolutely are out of the question, because that is not what I think and what I believe, and I don't want such charges to be put to you. That is an omission on my part, and I apologise to the Tribunal. It was my mistake for not reading it carefully and for not being careful, and maybe I wasn't sufficiently businesslike and cautious in signing something I hadn't read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in your own statement where it says -- I'll give you another Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. example of illegal collection of funds. At that time, the police was involved in organised car thefts, and you wrote in your own hand next to that, "Not true."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this and similar things are to be found in every paragraph. There is not a single paragraph without deletions, without additions or explanations to the entirely opposite effect. So these statements absolutely do not correspond to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation of the interview is not correct. When you say something that can fill three pages and it is then put into ten lines cannot be correct, and I can explain to you. If this was a closed session, I would tell you who was responsible. The conclusion is not correct. But there was one fact that was true about this car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your own hand, you continue to say: "Corrections should be made in keeping with my remarks and with these revisions and explanations should be handed to the accused providing him an explanation of the reasons for such errors, which are more than obvious, and I believe personally that it is not proper to charge him using such information and interpretations of what I said." And that's what you signed and dated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of this paper, you say: "Started to revise a part of this statement, making serious objections, but when he saw the statement translated into Serbian, investigator Gerald Sexton told him that he should not be doing that because he would have occasion to do so in The Hague during proofing."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in The Hague a couple of days ago you actually did not have enough time to read this through properly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had been given occasion to do so in Belgrade, there would be no need to discuss this now. We would not be wasting a single minute over it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we have gone through this series of your submissions regarding the illegalities in the work of certain people in your ministry, sloppy work --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bad organisation, poor skills, abuse of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Errors made in various departments in the provinces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Financial omissions, deficiencies, losses of property that remained unexplained because the management was not interested in finding out what happened to this property.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you tried to get these errors redressed. Do you remember that two ministers were actually arrested due to financial crime, white-collar crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about low-level employees. I'm talking about two ministers who were arrested for this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't remember this, but I take your word for it. Those who were involved in this, Mr. Milosevic, actually got promotions, and they still feature in our society while we are sitting here talking. Those who put us in this situation, us who asked you and other management to redress the situation and to work properly, we would perhaps not be rich but we would be living better if it had been done in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You discussed mainly matters that had to do with sloppiness, lack of professionality, certain conduct among people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also abuse in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that have to do with what we are discussing today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is relevant. I don't know. I didn't know what it would be used for, for what charges. I was just telling you what happened, and I see that your associates placed it in wrong hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as you know, such submissions are always forwarded from the cabinet of the president of the republic to the Prime Minister. You don't call that wrong hands, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I addressed it to him too, and you see how I ended up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your statement, page 4, paragraph 2, that the Assembly of Serbia decided to conduct an investigation and that you headed this investigation and found out in Kosovo that a lot of equipment, including weapons and ammunition, was stolen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was missing. And I handed my report to General Simovic personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you establish who stole the weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not given the opportunity. As far as I'm concerned --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The witness is alert to the fact that we are in public session and whether he has any concerns about the previous two questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say: "A lot of equipment, weaponry and ammunition was missing, stolen, including money. Kosovo, as an underdeveloped region, was receiving aid amounting to 1.5 million dollars per day."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from us. There is some confusion. They received aid, as an underdeveloped region, from all republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's from the federal budget.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, federal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One at a time. One at a time. You're giving evidence, Witness; remember that. And you're cross-examining, Mr. Milosevic, not having a conversation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. I'm glad for this opportunity to talk to this witness whom I had not known before, but I see that he was involved in this work, and he does not wish to perjure himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say on page 4, paragraph 3: "Many Serbs had already left this region." Tell me why.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they certainly didn't escape from anything good. They had to leave. I don't know if you mean Krajina or Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kosovo, Kosovo. You are talking about Kosovo in this part of your statement, because immediately after that you say that Kosovo was an underdeveloped region receiving aid and many Serbs had left it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the situation in Kosovo very well because I had visited it both as an inspector and on other business, and I am familiar with what was going on. The irredentists were not active starting from 1990s. They had been active for 50 years and more. So these problems go hand-in-hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mention the Karic brothers. They had claimed to the authorities that they were planning to build 30 to 50 companies for Serbs who wished to go on living in Pec. Do you know, since I am familiar with this myself, that they were famous for employing both Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is a free interpretation. I did not say this. I know Bogoljub Karic myself too as a businessman. All this is gossip that I heard. I never inspected his businesses, and they would not have been included in this statement if I had been given a chance to review this properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, although you didn't inspect and audit their businesses, that they had built universities, a foundation, schools, et cetera, and all of this in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know all of this. And I believe that this interpretation is improper. But I did say that they had received loans and that they had used them for promoting the economy. And if I had been given the chance to review my statement, this would not be included in it. I don't think this is worth discussing further. I believe this man is a businessman and that he used the money properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is still a renowned businessman, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the witness may have overlooked that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say - that is on page 5, paragraph 1 - that documents never indicated the names of persons who received the money, and the money was channelled through the SDK, the social accountancy service. The confidentiality of disbursements and the SDK do not go together. You as an expert must know this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. Why are we discussing this when I already confirmed this, Mr. Milosevic? And I have to tell you, you are perfectly right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I have seen here, and may I point this out to you, this claim that I together with Adzic and Simovic organised and planned clandestine financing, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me reply to this. They must have asked me who was responsible when things like this happen, and I must have answered, "If it's happening on a ship, it's the captain who is responsible." And in the state, I said, according to the normal chain of subordination, who is responsible? If it's the command of operation, it's the head of the General Staff. If it's the ministry, it's the minister. If it's about the state of Serbia, it must be you. And as for whether something is clandestine or not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you actually told them only that I was the president of Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you mention -- I don't want to this say because I don't want to go into private session, because this concerns a person who is a relative of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that he asked me to help resolve the housing problem of his relative who is a refugee, and I replied that there were 600.000 refugees that need to be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your Kum, your best man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean my daughter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Marija is his grandchild. And after that, he retired, in '83.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this something we can really call a matter of principle? A person who is working with me, or for me, asking me to help his relative and I told him we can't make exceptions, we have 600.000 refugees and we held them all equally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the only example. You know in Krnjak how many people were there. He had a brother there, and a sister, and cousins. Three generations of the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you stated here my reaction, and my reaction was that we have to treat everyone equally. There were 600.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife told me about this. It's her family. I'm telling you this is true, but this is not relevant. We are only wasting time. We can discuss this outside this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me, since you are involved --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not involved in anything. I'm a retired person now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are dealing with a budget in this statement. Tell me, please, you don't know what the budget was at the time, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The budget is a matter of public information. It was published in the Official Gazette of Serbia. I cannot discuss that. I don't use words like "black funds." I don't use such terms. I never did in my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear you say this, Witness 83.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the kind of terminology an expert uses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you say here there is a secret part of the budget which is called the black fund.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the question. If we were discussing football perhaps the term could have been used, but not here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also says in the statement that you said that this part of the budget was higher than the official budget.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was marked here as something that you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I crossed it out, saying that it was incorrect. And I also asked them to convey my apologies to you because I had no opportunity to read it previously. Please, this is not worth discussing, and I wrote specifically that this should not be a charge levelled against you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Evidence is what is given in this court. It's not what's in your statement. It doesn't matter what's in your statement. All that matters is what is said in this court. Now, Mr. Milosevic, you've got five minutes left. In my judgement, you've taken up your time dealing largely with matters which are of peripheral relevance at best, and it's entirely your own fault because you were told at the beginning how much time you had. Now, you've got five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May, but could you tell me what relevant matter I have not mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your conversation with an individual, for example, Witness. I don't want to have to go into private session so I won't mention the name, but a person that came to the ministry and you happened to meet that individual, and he asked the assistant minister, right, what had happened to his funds, to the resources.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The person that came from the diaspora, and I was already on sick leave --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. That's not what I'm referring to. I'm referring to the person who led the volunteers. And you say he asked what had happened to his resources.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, yes. I remember now. I understand; in the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, when you brought in your sick leave papers, as you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know that they were resources which were taken away from him, confiscated from him by the police, and in view of the right of volunteers to go, he asked that someone intervene to have these resources given back to him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know. What I do know I said here to the letter, and it was introduced into the statement and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally just spoke about the Red Star football team.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Red Star football team and Tigric. And I had a nice time discussing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So now we've cleared that point up. As you mentioned the participation of the diaspora in financing this aid and assistance, do you have any idea how much the diaspora, in fact what role it played in the financing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, but I just said that I was revolted and sick and explained to that man I was rather revolted, and I suppose he went to see the Prime Minister to set out the problems with him and see what the diaspora could do for its own people in the homeland. And I was revolted, and he was telling me of the situation. And he said, "What's -- why do you feel like that?" I said I felt inundated. When there's a flood, everything rises to the surface. So I write about these leaders who have come to the surface, delving in murky water. So one cannot be different from one's environment. And I'm sure you had problems too of the same kind, because you had people around you who should not have been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, as Mr. Nice presented a document here and the title was "Information about resources ensured by the budget by the republic for assistance to Serb regions in Croatia with a proposal for their implementation." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it clear that we're talking about financial assistance to the Serb regions in Croatia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also right that there wasn't a single man in Serbia who wasn't in favour of helping these people over these difficult times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And you personally and me personally too. But the irregularities came to the fore when people handled these resources. It wasn't professionally handled, and then the resources were devaluated and so on and there were other problems that these leaders had to face that they weren't up to facing. They weren't professionals in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So they are the ones you complain about; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little below the top echelons of your ministry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, actually they were in the topmost circles. They took decisions and were promoted for them. And they still have fared fairly well today too, they're not having a hard time of it, and we were -- not like us who were opposed to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in tab 4 we see a letter that was sent, and in the letter -- actually it comes from the Republika Srpska Krajina: "Because of the impossibility of directly transferring money to our transfer account, we have concluded a contract with work organisations whereby you will transfer money to their transfer accounts," et cetera, et cetera. Tell me now, please - that's all in tab 4 - is there anything there which was not aboveboard, if I can put it that way, dishonest in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the document for the first time here but that was a way of bridging the mistake, the gap in the interruption of payments flow, and I said yes, it was all right, that things should be done this way for the money to reach the ultimate destination and that this was the participant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice asked you something about the markings of the document, the numbers, and did it say "confidential," "strictly confidential," or whatever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I saw that it did say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We're not disputing that, but just tell me this now, please, as you worked there for a long time: Is it true and correct that at least 90 per cent of the documents throughout your years of service, all the decades you spent working in that ministry, that it was characteristic of that particular ministry of yours that 90 per cent of the documents would have "strictly confidential" written up at the top as a header?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the level of the people who determined the level of confidentiality was such that they were not able themselves to assess whether a document was actually confidential or not and they would err on the side of caution and put "strictly confidential" everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but that was the practice of decades.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everything would be termed "secret" or "strictly confidential" or the like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If that's the case, I can't ask all the questions I have here, although I'd like to have been able to ask this witness more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have liked that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you deal with documents, and you say that the Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia had no other source of financing but to receive funds from Serbia, or, rather, it's quite clear to you that they did have some sources themselves.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However that, without our assistance, they wouldn't have been able to survive.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my personal opinion that they would have had a hard time of it, a hard time surviving under such difficult circumstances at such difficult moments and that it was quite proper to lend assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, these two documents, tab 2, in fact, which relates to information about resources provided for by the budget of the republic for assistance to the Serb regions, and the other document, tab 3, it is the complaint, the submission with regards to illegal and inappropriate activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my next question deals with the documents that were brought up during the examination-in-chief, the ones that were requested, and you saw the documents which requires assistance of some kind. A document was mentioned asking for 92 million marks, German marks for example. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is, with respect to those documents, although there were others too, but my question is: Do you have any knowledge apart from knowing that this assistance was sought that you know that certain resources and funds were sent out towards regions outside the Republic of Serbia? Did you see documents to that effect and do you know how much money was sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have knowledge of that. I dealt with that personally. I opened some of those accounts personally in the branch offices, and I think it says so in the document, whether in that one or in other documents. I know it was in Knin, Novi Sad, et cetera. Therefore, I did know about that, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested here about these 92 million marks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marks aren't mentioned there. It's dinars that are stipulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, are -- is that the equivalent number of dinars corresponding to the 92 million German marks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't calculate the exchange rate now as it used to be at the time. I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing as we can with the first two documents that were produced in open session and that deal with the passage of money to the Serbs in Croatia and the suggestion that money was not being passed to kill people, the money that went, was that to serve members of the Territorial Defence? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-083 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-083, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. Just wait, if you would, while the blinds are brought down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening, may I repeat what I'm sure I've said at least twice before, so that the accused can have this in mind: Figures in the long, we hope helpful, witness schedule setting out the times that witnesses may take are estimates that we have to put in because we are trying to calculate what witnesses we can call. Wherever I'm in a position to take a witness more shortly or to ensure that one of my colleagues does, I will do so, either because it's possible to deal with the evidence more swiftly than one had previously calculated or because we will be cutting out from the evidence material that we had previously thought relevant but which we judge not to have sufficient relevance or not to be of such great relevance as to merit the time of the Court. So therefore, we will be focusing our efforts on calling from the maximum amount of evidence whatever is relevant and it may take nothing like the time set down beside the witnesses, and we would press the accused to prepare on the basis of focusing his attention on what is relevant first as well. Your Honour, that much for that. The next witness on the original list was to be a 92 bis witness. The Court will remember that yesterday I asked that we reverse the order, and I think that 92 bis witness is not yet here. The position is that if a 92 bis witness was taken, the accused would have to be dealing with both witnesses in cross-examination today in any event because the 92 bis witness would only take an hour, and I would ask to be allowed to call Audrey Budding next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you think you will be with the witness in direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could check to see if the witness 1102 is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, not yet. A few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago Mr. Nice said that an assessment of the time he gives doesn't represent any information. Why, then, are time estimates made at all? Isn't it logical and proper and correct that if an assessment of time is made and if you assess that it will last for as long as you assess, that this should be a piece of information for me to be able to plan how long my cross-examination might last? So what's the purpose of giving out information if it doesn't bind the person giving out the information to stand by what he does? There's no sense to it or any logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've heard the explanation which has been given. The time is put there for the Prosecution's internal planning. Now, it can only be regarded as an estimate to show the time which they estimate that the witness may take. It may assist you in trying to plan your examination, but it can't be anything more than that, and they certainly can't be bound by that particular figure. Now, the proposal at the moment is that Audrey Budding should be called. Now, do you want to say anything about that? Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there something you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, it's up to you who you're going to call and how. All I wish to clarify here is this: A moment ago, the piece of information we heard from Mr. Nice was that this particular witness, lady witness, called in here as an expert witness who will be testifying about some kind of historical background to Serb nationalism, which touches upon, as far as I can see, her interests going back to the fifteenth century, that she will be cross-examined -- examined-in-chief for half an hour. Let me say at the outset that for this particular witness, I'm going to need at least -- I'm going to need far more time, incomparably more time, and I think it is your duty to give me that time, because I do need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not the issue at the moment. Have you any objection or do you want to make any point about calling this witness next, as is proposed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's all the same to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If it's all the same to you, call the next witness. We will consider in due course when the examination-in-chief is finished how long there should be in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I don't want the accused --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't want the accused to languish under the misapprehension that we're trying in any way to disadvantage him. And it's a procedural matter that he doesn't focus on, I suspect: Expert witnesses fall under a different category. They are, as the Court knows, witnesses whose is typically tendered through their report and they may be subject to no examination-in-chief by the Prosecution. Where we do that, or where we take the evidence shortly, there is no suggestion on our part that the accused should be limited in cross-examination time to the short period of time we take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I don't want the accused, who is wont sometimes to impute motives to us, to think we're doing anything other than abide by the rules of the court and try to save time. Your Honour, I hope that the Court has the witness's expert report and her curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think I have a curriculum vitae to hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I suffered the same shortcoming last night, and I think it's now been recopied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there has been a revision to the report, for I observed comparatively recently that some of the footnotes in B/C/S had not been fully translated. There is, I think, a revised version for distribution, if the Chamber would find that helpful, depending on the degree to which they've marked the earlier version, but I gather that the page numbering of the body of the report is not in any way affected. May the report be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The new report should have the exhibit number on it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the new report with the end notes will be Prosecution Exhibit 508.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And may the witness's curriculum vitae be given a separate and perhaps following number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your full name Audrey Helfant Budding?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Associate at the Harvard Academy for International and Area Studies?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Educated at Swarthmore College in Greek, and Cambridge University in social and political sciences, and then at Harvard where you took your Ph.D in 1998, the dissertation being on "Serb Intellectuals and the National Question."

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes, all of that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have experience for the United States Foreign Service, inter alia, at the United States embassy in Belgrade between 1987 and 1990?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you taught and published on various matters, including on aspects of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, at the invitation and instruction of the Office of the Prosecutor, prepare a report for use in this case headed "Serbian Nationalism in the Twentieth Century, Historical Background and Context"?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has that publication been available publicly, it having been filed publicly at this court?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, it's been available for critics to make comments on it, those comments no doubt being available to the accused and his team if they had sought them; correct?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's Mrs. Budding?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes. Or Dr. Budding, as you prefer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Dr. Budding then. And I'm only -- because your report's been available to and read by the parties, I'm just going to ask you a few questions, and in each topic - perhaps at most half a dozen - I would ask you to confine your answers to a limited number of sentences, just a few minutes, so you can provide the overview on a particular topic that I seek. And first, you're an historian and, of course, you come here simply not to argue any point adverse to the accused but to provide a background source for the Chamber and the parties to consider. With your knowledge of the history of Yugoslavia and your knowledge of the general topics we are dealing with here, and a mind to your report generally, what topics, in your judgement as an historian, should we have in mind in approaching our task?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: If I could choose a single historical concept that I believe helps in the understanding of contemporary events in the Balkans, it would be the concept of the frontier society; that this is a region where empires and, later, great powers have clashed repeatedly over the centuries, and the consequences of this for the peoples of the Balkans are twofold. One is simply the very extensive migrations of peoples that occurred throughout the early modern era, meaning that people, the populations of many regions become confessionally mixed; later, as people gained national consciousness, nationally mentioned. The second major consequence for the peoples of the Balkans is contained in what I call in the report the repetition of cycles of status reversal. In other words, that each new ruler favoured co-nationals, or co-religionist, that each new change of regime privileged certain groups and suppressed or oppressed others, with the result that intercommunal relations on the ground, if you will, however favourable at the local or village level, were repeatedly overwhelmed by these larger political events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving through selected passages of your report in an orderly fashion, we would find on page 10 reference to something that's been raised by the accused in respect of Drenica and what happened there at or after the Second World War. In a few sentences and in light of the way that's been raised, can you help us with what your research into Drenica reveals.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the speakers to please slow down because this is very succinct subject matter, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I mentioned briefly in the report, first of all, at the end of the Second World War, it was re-incorportated into the Yugoslav state by the Partisans against very substantial resistance on the part of the Albanian population. Specifically with reference to Drenica, that was the scene of a revolt by an Albanian leader Shaban Polluzha, who had originally been a part of the Albanian National Front, the Balli Kombetar, had later in the war joined the Partisans and in fact been authorised by them to mobilise troops for Partisan forces in the Drenica region. He did so in approximately the late fall of 1944, but in January of 1945, he and his men revolted against the Partisans, refusing to be sent to the Srem front north of Belgrade, and this revolt was put down with substantial bloodshed. We don't have exact numbers, but the sources suggest that perhaps a few thousand of the Albanians may have been killed, some in battle, and some in summary executions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 14 of your report, you observe that over the 30 years preceding Yugoslavia's collapse, you will argue that every decline, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cultural or political, in Yugoslavia, evoked mobilisation of all Serbs and more specifically that the weakening of Yugoslav unity immediately and dramatically focused attention on nationally-minded Serbs within Serbia on the position of Serbs outside Serbia. Can you give us one or, if time permits, two examples of that?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Well, when I refer to that process, it ties in with my larger point about the emergence of a certain Serbian national mind set, that is a set of beliefs related to the Serbian question in Yugoslavia, and a central component of that belief was that if Yugoslavia was not to exist as a unified state, as a state that might unite all Serbs, then Serbia ought to attempt to protect or unite, if not all Serbs, at least as many Serbs as possible. This phenomenon is very visible in the period of Yugoslavia's dissolution. The main earlier parallel that I see has to do with the late 1960s, the period of extensive decentralisation based on the constitutional amendments. And at that time, the idea was raised in discussions, for instance, at the Belgrade law faculty, that if Yugoslavia was to be decentralised, as it would be by those amendments, that then Serbia's borders should be changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The accused may have stated first his position on the change of Yugoslavia's borders in 1990. This can be, I think, referenced on pages 35 and 64 of the report. Can you help us with how that was received in Yugoslavia or what reaction to it was predictable in your judgement?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Well, in June of 1990, as I state in the report, Mr. Milosevic first raised the possibility of Serbian border changes in connection with discussions of the new Serbian constitution. I would say that the reaction outside Serbia was one of consternation in large part because people were fully aware of the degree to which the Yugoslav populations lived intermingled. In other words, that there was really no way to enlarge Serbia's borders to include Serbs and only Serbs. With reference to whether these reactions were predictable, I think entirely so. And in fact, in the report I cite a statement from 20 plus years earlier, Dobrica Cosic's statement at the 14th plenum of the Central Committee of the Serbian party where he suggested in the context of the constitutional discussion of the constitutional amendments that if the process of state formation within Yugoslavia were to be continued, the Serbian people would also seek a single state, that the political -- the consequences of this needed no political imagination to foresee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pages 57 and 58 of your report you make reference to the accused's brinkmanship and violation of the rules of the game of Yugoslavian politics, of Yugoslav politics. Can you explain that a little further?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: When I made that statement I had in mind primarily events between the summer of 1998 and the collapse of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia in January of 1990. That's the period that came to be known as the Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution; in other words, the use of mass meetings of citizens to overthrow the leaderships of the province of Vojvodina and of the Republic of Montenegro as well as the substantial abrogation of Kosovo's autonomy through the -- through the constitutional amendments of spring 1989, which made possible the reduction of the province's autonomy in the new constitution of 1990. I think that I characterise this as brinkmanship first because this showed Mr. Milosevic's willingness to push for a somewhat decentralised Yugoslavia at all costs, even at the risk of alienating others from the existing Yugoslav state. I think that it's very clear that they in fact had that effect, specifically the fall of the Montenegrin leadership in response to crowd pressure was seen by republican leaders outside Serbia as deeply threatening, as perhaps opening the door to further exploitation of the Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution into other republics, specifically with regard to the rules of the political game in Yugoslavia, that that is the accepted rules of political conduct. One of the most of these was the principle known as reaching agreement or "usaglasavanje," which was a principle central to the 1974 constitution. Clearly, using mobilised popular support to overthrow leaders of other republics was entirely contrary to this principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I turn to a couple of questions about Kosovo, is it possible, briefly, to trace in a way that may be of assistance to understanding how people were thinking, the concept of all Serbs living within one state and to use that as a generalised concept rather than any label that may from time to time be attached to it?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Well, as I state in the report, the idea of collecting all the people in one state is not in any way unique to Serbian nationalism. It's really the principle that's central to all nationalisms, that cultural and political borders ought to coincide. In my view, this element of Serbian nationalism became particularly destructive and self-destructive at the end of the twentieth century because Serbs in the course of the nineteenth century had sought a unified state. And whether this was to be a state of Serbs or South Slavs was really not clearly stated. This, in the nineteenth century, historically what happened was a process of simple expansion of the Serbian state. This process was overtaken by the events of the First World War which made possible the establishment of a Yugoslav state on the basis of South Slav territories of the Habsburg Monarchy being combined with the independent state of Serb, and the consequence of this process, I would say, was that the idea of where the borders of Serbia should be was never fully internalised among Serbs. I think I can make that point clearer if I might be allowed a brief comparison. Many states in the Balkans and elsewhere have various state projects greater; greater this, smaller this. If we were to take the example of Bulgaria at the beginning of the twentieth century, Bulgarian nationalism consistently, and in many instances aggressively, sought a greater Bulgaria to include large parts of Macedonia. By the end of the twentieth century, this concept had been politically marginalised among other reasons because Bulgaria had chosen the losing side in two world wars in pursuit of its territorial claims. The process in Serbia was very different because in entering the Yugoslav state, Serbian borders were not defined in the international sense, and when the Yugoslav state collapsed, the borders of the Republic of Serbia were in many, although not instances, not perceived by Serb populations inside and outside Serbia as the legitimate borders of Serbdom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Kosovo's autonomy, the changes in that autonomy, what effect, in your judgement, did they have on the federal constitutional and political structure? This is dealt with on various pages in the report, but about 41, 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: First, if we consider the status that Kosovo and of course Vojvodina as the other autonomous province had in the constitution of 1974, they were defined as constituent elements of the federation, and that was carried through very consistently at the federal level. The provinces, exactly like the republics, had one representative on the federal collective Presidency. The provinces in both Chambers of the federal parliament had their own delegations, and although these delegations were smaller than those of the republics, this had very little practical significance given the requirement for reaching agreement by -- by agreement of all the delegations on most important questions. Therefore, it was impossible that the Serbian leadership could change the relation of the autonomous provinces to Serbia in the constitutional sense without simultaneously changing the balance of power at the federal level. And the specific effect of the curtailment of the autonomy of the provinces, of the replacement of fairly independent provincial leaderships with leaders who were under the influence of Mr. Milosevic meant that the balance of power at the federal level was greatly changed, that after that and the anti-bureaucratic revolution in Montenegro, Serbia in effect controlled the votes of four members of the federal Presidency, of four delegations in each house of the federal parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I've got three more topics as short as the ones we've already covered. Bosnia-Herzegovina: In your judgement, how did that fit into both Serbian and, if it helps us by way of contrast, Croatian national thought?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Well, there are certainly parallels between Serbian and Croatian national claims on the territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Most important, both Serbs and Croats have historically claimed Muslims as members of their own nation, simply differing confessionally and in many instances have not accepted the idea of Muslims or Bosniaks as a separate national group. I see some contrast between Serbian and Croatian national claims on Bosnia in that the Croatian claims have often made more use of historical arguments and as a corollary have generally denied the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a historical entity, whereas the Serbian arguments have often made more use of ethnic claims. Logically so, I think, since the Serbian claims on Bosnia arrive -- arise particularly in the last few decades of the nineteenth century at a time when Serbs made up the largest single group of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Budding, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes to take a short break. Could you please remember, as we have to warn all witnesses, during the adjournment and any others there may be in your case, during your evidence, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before you resume, one or two administrative matters. We have to deal with argument on 92 bis witness statements for the remaining witnesses on Bosnia, Bijeljina, Zvornik, et cetera. We must find time for that argument this week. There are also motions for the admission of transcripts in relation to Visegrad and Brcko, one of the witnesses being scheduled to come next week. So we ought to deal with that on Monday morning at the latest, hear the argument about those transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I foresee it as a possibility that we could conclude this week's listed witnesses before the end of Friday. We're already making arrangements to advance next Monday's witness to Friday. Although I shan't be here on Friday, Mr. Groome can deal with the Bosnian arguments generally then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. If you would alert him to that, dealing with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other point is that we shall lose an hour and a half next week because we finish on Friday at 12.00. We must try and find an additional hour and a half during the week. If you can bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may raise a matter on the legal argument. We filed detailed submissions in relation to all these matters. I won't be here tomorrow because of the other legal work I'm undertaking on the case. I don't think there is any further elaboration which is needed from the written documents that have been already filed by the amici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Budding, I think it has gone up from what was forecast as two topics to about three. The ante-penultimate being the SANU memorandum, of which you write extensively in your report, starting at page 53, and of which the Chamber has already heard quite an amount of evidence, but in brief, its significance, and if you can also offer some assistance for those of us who don't come from single state countries with academies, the role of an academy in this setting.

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Well, if I might address the second part of the question first. I think that intellectuals, and particularly intellectual institutions, have had in Eastern Europe a political importance that can be rather hard to understand if you're coming from a different system, in part because intellectuals served as spokesmen for the nation in the nineteenth century against, in many cases, multinational empires. And because their participation in politics was much more common and at a higher level than is common in Western countries, I would say in large part because in many parts of Eastern Europe the educated class was relatively small so the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. same people would very frequently be university professors, then government ministers, then back to professors. The Serbian academy specifically was certainly seen as the most prestigious intellectual institution of Serbia and one might say more broadly of the Serbian people, which clearly gave its pronouncements a great importance. Now, to turn to the memorandum itself, I think that it is important to note that the document known as the memorandum was a draft which was not adopted by any body of the academy because it was leaked to the press and work on it was stopped while it was still in the draft stages. Having said that, in many ways the memorandum presents a very developed statement of what I have referred to as a mind-set about the Serbian national question in the mid 1980s. In my view, the most important part of the memorandum from this point of view is its very one-sided emphasis on Serbian victimisation, the presentation of the decentralisation of Yugoslavia as uniquely damaging to Serbs, the overstatement in regard to the difficulties faced by Serbs in Kosovo, the characterisation of Serbs in Kosovo as exposed to genocide were, in my view, exaggerated and one-sided statements. And finally, to conclude the memorandum's significance, although it certainly does not set out a post-Yugoslav national programme, it suggests that the existing Yugoslavia is so damaging for Serbia and for Serbs that Serbia must look to its own interests which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Budding, may I ask you on what do you base your conclusion that the characterisation of Serbs in Kosovo and their victimisation was exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if we look at specifically the statistics for serious crimes committed in Kosovo in the 1980s, the instances of rape and murder, the most serious crimes, were actually lower than the Yugoslav average. I think that genocide is not a word that can be used in the absence of wide-scale killing. If I might expand slightly on the difficulties faced by Serbs in Kosovo, I think that there were certainly some acts of intimidation, including some acts of violence, but that these simply did not at that time reach the level that could be described fairly as genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Budding, you were -- thank you. Dr. Budding, you were in the process of explaining that although the memorandum didn't set out a post-Yugoslav national programme, it's suggested that the existing Yugoslavia was so damaging for Serbia and for Serbs that Serbia should look to its own interests, and then you were about to conclude that sentence, I think.

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Thank you. I was going to suggest that the memorandum and certain other things that appear around the same time represent a real novelty in the Serbian attitude towards Yugoslavia, that up until that time the predominant attitude had been that Serbs had a special interest in Yugoslavia, that Yugoslavia was in some sense indispensable to Serbs. I see in the memorandum, as many contemporary observers did, the beginnings of a Serbian turning away from Yugoslavia as an optimal solution to the Serbian national problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 69 of your report, you deal with the 28th of March, 1991, meeting of the presidents. You explain at the foot of that page that the accused's basic stance was that Yugoslavia's dissolution was possible only upon the basis of self-determination of peoples carried out through national referenda, somewhat otherwise unspecified. Can you comment further on that and would you like to comment on what a referendum of the Muslims would have appeared like?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Well, to me, the basic point about the call for national referendums is that it was entirely impractical in the Yugoslav context. It's simply impossible to imagine how it could have been carried through in nationally mixed areas, and certainly many people in Serbia, as elsewhere, were fully aware of that. I include in my report a sentence that Zoran Djindjic had written in the summer of 1990, where he suggested that if the land could shake in Yugoslavia with the wish of its inhabitants to go elsewhere with their land, that some parts of Yugoslavia would experience a permanent earthquake. So that to me the main point to be made about the idea of national referendums is that it's simply impossible to see how it could have been carried through. If there had at that time -- if such an attempt had been made at the time -- you ask specifically about what the Muslim stance might have been. My guess would certainly be that the majority would have chosen at that point to remain within Yugoslavia because Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia were specifically the two republics that tried hardest to find some sort of compromise solution to enable the continued existence of Yugoslavia in some form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the foot of the same page, 70, picking up from that and the top of the very last page of your report you quote Alija Izetbegovic at the same meeting asking the question and someone would have to explain what a national referendum means, and what, for him, was the predictability or predictable result? If you would like to just comment on that before we come to my very last question.

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Well, what he said was someone would have explain to me what a national referendum would mean in Sarajevo where there were large numbers of Muslims, of Serbs, of Croats, and he answered his own question, saying a referendum and then we would be shooting at each other from the windows. I think he saw the absurdity of the idea. If I might expand very slightly on that point. I think that he recognised there a truth that the idea of the national referendum was simply not applicable to the urban populations. There were some rural areas where it might have been possible to draw territorial borders along ethnic lines, but in the major cities - in Zagreb with 100.000 Serbs, as well as in Sarajevo with perhaps 170.000 - this was, in my view, a meaningless concept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally - this is a question you may feel you've answered sufficiently already in your reference to the clash of civilisations - but in a case where we're concerned not only with the acts and thoughts, for example, of the accused but also the acts and thoughts of individuals, you of course have the long history at your fingertips, others less so, but whether it's the long history or the more recent history of the genocide of the Serbs as you I think yourself would describe it in the Second World War --

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- how significant, in your judgement, may some aspects of history be in understanding the thinking of the various participants?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: If I might, before turning to my main answer to your question, simply address the phrase "clash of civilisations" very briefly. I would not characterise my presentation of the problem as clash of civilisations, simply because that term is very often used to imply that, for instance, Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim people, by virtue of being Orthodox, Catholic, Muslim, being of incompatible nations and simply cannot live together. So my presentation of the clash of empires and great powers in the region was meant in a different sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: As far as the way that -- what one might call historically shaped frames of mind influenced the events of the 1990s, in my view the single most important aspect is the availability within living memory of what some scholars have called crisis frames; that is, that even though people are living in nationally mixed environments, are working with people of other nations, are frequently marrying them, their social reality may be multinational, they at the same time have - particularly of course in the memory of the Second World War - a vivid idea that things can be very different, that there's an alternate reality that may exist and can be called forth, and I think that helped to shape the events of the post-Yugoslav wars and the dissolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Budding, you will be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can have the rest of today - perhaps if we go a little after quarter to - and you can have the first session tomorrow morning, and if you ask for more, we would review the position, but you can have two and a half hours, something of that order, if that assists you in preparing your cross-examination. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I must tell you straight away that this time is absolutely inadequate to cross-examine this witness who has filed a very extensive report dealing with historical issues, and I request you to give me the whole day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's start and see how we get on before we decide anything like that. Judge Robinson has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you start, Mr. Milosevic, I wanted to ask Dr. Budding something about the last comment that she made. The influence of the reality of the Second World War. I think you said that although people with different ethnicities were living together, they had with them at that time what you call an alternate reality that may exist and can be called forth. So are you then saying that during the Tito period, where the different ethnic groups were held together by Tito, that there was always present this -- the concept of this alternate reality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's quite a complicated question, Your Honour. I think that it was not necessarily present in people's conscious minds. In fact, if you look at how people who had themselves lived through the Second World War chose to address it, many of them chose not to discuss it with their children in any way, and so those children, I think, would not at that point have had that present in their minds. I think that it was -- it was there, submerged, depending very much on which part of the country we're talking about and how much destruction that part of the country had experienced during the war. I think that the problem was greatly compounded by the fact that there was no free and fact-based discussion of the Second World War in Titoist Yugoslavia but, rather, an extremely ideological presentation of the Partisan conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll probably come back to that during the cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Budding, it was said at the outset that in addition to this report which you titled "Serbian Nationalism in the Twentieth Century," four years earlier, that is in 1998, you defended your doctoral thesis, titled "Serb Intellectuals and the National Question, 1961-1991." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AUDREY BUDDING
utterances.text: Yes.
